meta.tagline: A digital twin of the physical exhibition — stones, scans, and cryptography.

hero.title: Speaking Matter
hero.sub: A digital twin of the physical exhibition. The visitor moves through four stations — touch, code, vault, fiction — and watches matter transform into data, and back.

station-1.title: Stamps press into clay.
station-1.body:
The Gesture

When a hand grasps a stone and presses it into soft clay, it repeats an ancient gesture of witness.

The stone's three-dimensional scan becomes a stamp — a personal claim on the place where it rests. Here the stamp itself carries a notarial signature: the unique gesture of a hand, unique style, transmitted through the stone's local topography — its own partial, intimate geography.

From Data to Tool

To translate raw surface into active tool:

  1. Stones gathered from different places across the land were scanned in three dimensions
  2. The digital model underwent voxelization (volume discretization)
  3. Precise cutting of the relief layer
  4. Boolean union with a grip handle for the human hand
  5. Finally printed in three-D

The result is a stamp that preserves in its head the original stone's topography to millimeter accuracy — every grain, every scratch, every geological wrinkle.

Positive and Negative

Two kinds of objects were created:

Positive Stamp: Where the stone's relief projects outward, asserting the stone itself. When pressed to clay, it leaves its mark — the stone's presence made visible.

Negative Stamp: The inverse pattern — a void pressed within a cylinder, into which clay sinks. It receives the impression, completing a circuit. The positive carries the stone's presence; the negative receives its absence.

Together, they complete a circle of impression and imprint, like seal and wax.

The Meeting

When the stamp presses into natural clay, two geological times meet:

  • Stone formed millions of years ago
  • Soft clay receiving its signature in this moment

Through the act of stamping, the person claims identity through the local stone. The mute makes itself heard through the speaker, and leaves in the world a physical fingerprint of place.
station-1.label: A stone becomes a seal. When stamped into clay, it bridges geological time — ancient rock meets receptive earth. These stamps transform a place's unique geology into a gesture of ownership, a notarized signature written in texture and time.

station-2.title: Surface becomes signal.
station-2.body:
The Translation

When a computer reads a stone, it sees no shape, no color, no story.

It sees numbers.

The Data

The elevation map from the stone's scan is a matrix of topographic measurements — thousands of samples from surface, from 0 (valley) to 1 (peak). This is the raw language of geology: pure topology, unmediated.

In Stone Code, this matrix is flattened into a continuous stream of bytes and displayed as a dense table, like a Hex Editor reading raw computer memory. Each row exposes 48 bytes of data, organized across four parallel dimensions:

Four Readings

OFFSET The precise position of the point in the overall data sequence. A coordinate in the stone's numerical body.

HEX VALUES
The data itself. Each byte appears as a pair of hexadecimal digits, colored in green. The intensity of the green derives from physical height: - Peaks glow bright green - Valleys sink into darkness

The color is not arbitrary: it is the stone's own height rendered as light.

DECODED
The numeric values forced into translation as characters: Greek letters, mathematical symbols, graphic blocks. Dense rows create a kind of cybernetic cuneiform — a language derived only from topography. The stone speaks in symbols it never meant to speak.

BITS
The binary checksum of the row (XOR), shown as a sequence of lit and dark blocks. A heartbeat. A pulse. A rhythm encoded in the stone's data.

The Header

At the screen's head floats metadata header: raw material facts —

  • Vertex count
  • Elevation range
  • Entropy measure
  • SHA-256 hash — the stone's cryptographic fingerprint

Change one byte, the cipher shifts entirely. The stone's identity is compressed into a single string.

The Reading

The resulting image reads like a classified document, like a terminal screen, like ancient text decoded — yet all it displays is raw stone surface data.

The mute speaks, just not in our language.

But perhaps in reading this code, we finally listen — not to stone's voice, but to its signature, its proof of existence rendered in the only language the machine will accept.
station-2.label: What happens when we force stone to speak in hexadecimal? Stone Code displays the raw topographic data of a scanned rock as a dense terminal output — cryptographic hashes, color-coded heights, binary pulses. The stone becomes readable, but at the cost of all meaning.

station-3.title: Encrypt with a stone.
station-3.body:
The Premise

Can a stone keep a secret?

The elevation map of each scanned stone is a field of random values — natural entropy created across millions of years of geological process. This randomness is not noise; it is data, as specific and unique as a fingerprint.

Geological Cryptography harnesses this randomness to generate a unique encryption key: 256 bits derived only from one stone's specific topography.

The Process

Step 1: Sampling The elevation map is sampled and converted to binary sequence — thousands of height measurements flattened into a stream of 1s and 0s.

Step 2: Error Correction Rescanning the same stone is never perfectly identical due to differences in light, angle, and resolution. A "fuzzy extractor" algorithm is applied — it generates public helper data that allows reconstruction of the exact same key even from a slightly different scan.

The helper data are safe to publish: they are worthless without the physical stone itself.

Step 3: Encryption The key feeds into AES-256 encryption — the same standard protecting banking records and classified intelligence. The stone becomes a cryptographic anchor.

The Application

In the Stone Vault app:

  1. User selects a physical stone
  2. User enters a message
  3. The stone encrypts it using its unique geological key
  4. Only whoever holds that specific stone can decrypt

The geological material becomes cryptographic material. The mute becomes the keeper of secrets.

The Paradox

A stone that has held silent for millions of years now holds silence of another kind: secrets locked within its surface. The encryption is not imposed from outside — it emerges from the stone's own history. You cannot fake it. You cannot duplicate it. The stone, in its opacity, becomes transparent to mathematics.
station-3.label: Stone as vault. The random topography of a rock surface, sculpted over millions of years, encodes a cryptographic key. Messages entrusted to this stone can only be unlocked by the stone itself — making geology the guardian of secrets.

station-4.title: Stones that never were.
station-4.body:
The Question

What happens when a limestone from the Galilee wears the skin of basalt from the Golan? When Jerusalem stone dresses in the texture of coastal kurkar?

This station explores a question: What is a stone's identity — its form or its surface? Its body or its skin?

The Premise

Each three-dimensionally scanned stone is a duality: geometry (the volumetric shape) and texture (the image wrapping that volume). In an act of "skin-swapping," one stone's surface is UV-mapped onto another stone's skeleton. One body, borrowed skin.

But surface exchange is only the beginning.

The Process

These hybrid forms undergo three layers of algorithmic distortion:

  1. Geometric warping — subtle twists and bends
  2. Fractal noise — perturbation along the surface normal
  3. Perlin noise — creating micro-texture at the smallest scale

The skin stretches and deforms with the geometry, like flesh on a body in flux. Texture and form become inseparable, as if the borrowed surface has learned to inhabit the new host.

The Result

Possible stones — forms carrying the visual memory of two real stones, yet whose bodies have wandered into impossible territory.

A geological fiction: stones that could have formed, but never did. Expression of drift, blurred boundaries, and the mixing of local identities. These are the stones that exist only in the space between two places, wearing two names.
station-4.label: When a stone wears another's skin, what remains of its identity? Possible Stones explores the boundary between form and surface, geology and fiction. By swapping textures between stones from different landscapes, we ask: can a stone carry the memory of a place it never came from?
